New Mexico property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • County assessors mail Notices of Valuation by around April 1 each year under Section 7-38-20; the net taxable value on the notice is the basis of the county treasurer's tax bill. (Property Tax : Individuals (NM Taxation and Revenue Department); source)
  • A protest petition is filed with the county assessor; in most cases it is due thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation (the later of April 1 or that 30-day date applies to the general rule). (Information Pamphlet for Property Valuation Protests (2024), NMSA 7-38-21; source)
  • A property owner may protest the assessor's value, classification, allocation of value, or denial of an exemption or limitation on increase in value by filing a petition with the assessor. (Information Pamphlet for Property Valuation Protests (2020); source)
  • The assessor schedules a hearing before the county valuation protests board and notifies the owner by certified mail at least fifteen days before the hearing. (Information Pamphlet for Property Valuation Protests (2020); source)
  • A protestant appeals a county valuation protests board decision by filing a notice of appeal with the district court for the county where the hearing was held, within the time set by Section 39-3-1.1 NMSA (Sections 7-38-28 and 39-3-1.1 and Rule 1-074 NMRA). (3.6.7.37 NMAC, as reproduced in the TRD Protest Pamphlet (2024); source)
  • The percentage of value against which tax rates are assessed shall not exceed thirty-three and one-third percent. (Information Pamphlet for Property Valuation Protests (2020); source)
  • Residential value in a tax year may not exceed the higher of 103% of the prior year's value or 106.1% of the value two years prior, unless a change of ownership occurred in the immediately prior year (NMSA 7-36-21.2). (Information Pamphlet for Property Valuation Protests (2024); source)
  • Delinquent property tax auctions are held annually as title research is completed, not in all 33 counties each year, usually at the county courthouse or a location designated by TRD. (Delinquent Property Tax Auctions : Businesses (NM TRD); source)
  • Bidding is oral; bidders must be physically present or represented by an agent. (Delinquent Property Tax Auctions : Businesses (NM TRD); source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A New Mexico deed is recorded with the county office named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • A quitclaim deed to quiet title or clear boundary disputes is exempt from the residential property transfer affidavit required by 7-38-12.1. (NMSA 7-38-12.1, as quoted in HB0342 (2025); source)
  • Electronic recording of real property instruments is governed by 1.11.2 NMAC: filers must enter a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the county clerk to become an authorized filer. (1.11.2 NMAC, Real Property Electronic Recording; source)
  • The MOU must require payment of recordation taxes, recording fees or clerk's fees assessed by statute, comply with notarization requirements, and provide a receipt notification including date and time of receipt. (1.11.2 NMAC; source)
  • Electronic instruments are rejected if they fail image/file-format specifications, security requirements, New Mexico statute requirements, or the clerk's requirements. (1.11.2 NMAC; source)

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

This guide covers what official sources say about New Mexico transfer on death deeds.

What the official sources say

  • An owner of New Mexico real estate may execute a deed designating a beneficiary who becomes owner on the owner's death; the deed can be revoked or amended at any time without the beneficiary's consent or knowledge. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)
  • The deed confers no ownership rights on the beneficiary until the owner dies; at death the beneficiary files a copy of the death certificate with the county clerk where the real estate is located and title passes without probate. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)
  • Transfer on death deeds have been available in New Mexico since June 2001 and can only be used for real estate located in New Mexico. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)
  • A 'small estate' is one worth less than $50,000 that does not include real property; it can be distributed without probate by an Affidavit of Successor in Interest if at least 30 days have passed since death and no probate has been filed. (Probate (NM Courts self-represented litigant guide); source)
  • If the estate includes real property, the personal representative may need to execute a Personal Representative's deed to transfer the property out of the decedent's name. (Probate (NM Courts self-represented litigant guide); source)
  • Probate may be filed in the probate court of the county where the decedent was domiciled, any time between 5 days and 3 years after death; the filing cost is $30. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)

New Mexico probate runs through the courts named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • A 'small estate' is one worth less than $50,000 that does not include real property; it can be distributed without probate by an Affidavit of Successor in Interest if at least 30 days have passed since death and no probate has been filed. (Probate (NM Courts self-represented litigant guide); source)
  • If the estate includes real property, the personal representative may need to execute a Personal Representative's deed to transfer the property out of the decedent's name. (Probate (NM Courts self-represented litigant guide); source)
  • Probate may be filed in the probate court of the county where the decedent was domiciled, any time between 5 days and 3 years after death; the filing cost is $30. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)
  • Probate is not needed for real estate held in joint tenancy or with a recorded Transfer on Death Deed. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)
  • A surviving spouse may transfer title to a community property home titled only in the deceased spouse's name by affidavit, filed six months after the death. (Probate - Self-Representation (NM Courts); source)
